Period schedule:

Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem — Read-Aloud and First Look

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Recite (p.1): teacher-led read-aloud of the full poem with illustrations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the textbook illustrations (p.1) of a man searching for his spectacles. Students observe and share what they notice about the pictures — what is the man doing, how does the child look?
Let us Recite — teacher reads the poem aloud expressively, pointing to illustrations for each stanza. Students listen with books open, following along.
Teacher reads the poem a second time, pausing after each stanza to invite students to echo the last line chorally. Emphasis on the bouncy four-beat rhythm.
Students attempt an unhurried read-aloud of the poem with the teacher as a whole class, using gestures for 'searched', 'glanced', and 'looked'. Teacher notes fluency and expression.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's humour rests on the child discovering the spectacles on Papa's head — let the final stanza land with a pause before students read it aloud, so the punchline can be felt. The bouncy anaphoric rhythm ('He can't…', 'He checked…') helps even hesitant readers join in. Encourage expressive gestures from the very first read-through.
materials: Blackboard or chart for key vocabulary (spectacles, glanced, searched)

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — What Did Papa Do?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.2): discuss and answer three short-answer questions about the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites two or three students to recite a stanza each from the poem (books open), refreshing the class's feel for the events before discussion begins.

Let us Think A — teacher poses Question 1 ('What is Papa searching for?') and Question 2 ('What are the possible places where Papa can find it?') as oral discussion prompts. Students respond in turns; teacher draws out textual evidence from stanzas two and three.

Teacher poses Question 3 ('At last, where does Papa find his lost item?'). Students locate the final stanza, discuss the child's role, and then write individual answers in their notebooks for all three questions.
Three to four students share their written answers aloud. Teacher provides brief corrective feedback on sentence structure and guides the class to agree on a model answer for each question.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read and chanted the poem together, students can now locate answers in specific stanzas — encourage them to point to the line in the text before speaking. A common difficulty is that students may say Papa found the spectacles 'on his head' without naming the child who told him — guide them to include both the discovery and the child's role. Answers should be in complete sentences.

periods.activity_title: Think, Discuss and Share — Gratitude and Home Talk

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (pp.2–3): guided discussion on chores, gratitude, and misplaced-things tables.
Let us Speak (p.3): share words for 'father' in home languages and discuss.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B, Question 1 — teacher asks students to think of chores Papa cannot do without spectacles (beyond reading). Students brainstorm in pairs, then share aloud; teacher lists ideas on the board.

Let us Think B, Question 2 and Table — students individually fill in the two tables (things misplaced at home, things misplaced at school; who helps find them). Pairs then discuss how they would express gratitude to those helpers.

Whole-class sharing: four to five students report one row from their table and demonstrate how they would thank the helper — verbally, with a gesture, or both. Teacher facilitates, affirming varied responses.

Let us Speak — teacher explains that 'Papa' is one English word for father. Students say aloud their own home-language word for father. Each student writes one or two words in their notebook; four to five students share with the class and a class list is built on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed Papa's frantic search in the poem, students now connect that domestic scene to their own homes — guide them toward specific, realistic chores (cooking, driving) rather than abstract ideas. The gratitude discussion works best when students practise an actual sentence or phrase rather than just listing it. Accept home-language words for 'father' warmly; celebrating the variety reinforces the poem's familial warmth.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.8): teacher reads word pairs aloud; students encircle pairs that sound different.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the task: she will read pairs of words aloud; students must listen and decide whether the two words sound the same or different, then encircle pairs that sound different. Students open textbooks to p.8 and locate the word-pair list.

Let us Listen — teacher reads each pair aloud three to four times at a clear, steady pace: pair-peer, fair-fare, sun-son, knot-note, ate-eight, hair-hare, deer-dear, dare-dear, bed-bad, fair-fear, cold-could, wood-would, knot-not, where-were, heal-heel, fill-feel. After each pair, students mark their answer.

Teacher re-reads the full list; this time she pauses after each pair and calls on students to say aloud whether the pair sounds the same or different and why. Class arrives at agreed answers together.

Brief consolidation: teacher writes four or five of the trickiest pairs on the board (e.g. sun-son, wood-would) and students say them together in unison, noting that same-sounding, different-meaning words are called homophones.

periods.teacher_notes: This is an aural task — the teacher's read-aloud is the stimulus, so pace and clarity matter more than speed. Homophones such as 'sun-son' and 'wood-would' are often confused; students who rely on spelling rather than sound may struggle, so ask them to close their eyes and just listen on the first read of each pair. The word 'homophone' is introduced lightly here as a label, not as a formal definition to memorise.

periods.activity_title: Word Work — Ascending Order and Pair Phrases

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.3): arrange groups of words in ascending order by size or weight.
Let us Learn B (p.4): fill in 'a pair of ___' phrases using picture clues.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'Handkerchief — Towel — Bedsheet — Sari' on the board and asks students to decide which is smallest. The class discusses the idea of arranging words by size or weight — ascending order is introduced with a simple physical gesture (hand rising).

Let us Learn A — students work through all five groups in their notebooks: fabric items, fruits, numbers, birds, and animals. After completing each group, a student reads the order aloud and the class confirms or corrects.
Students write two original examples of their own following the same ascending-order pattern. Two students share their examples with the class.

Let us Learn B — teacher holds up the textbook to show the pictures on p.4 and says the phrase 'a pair of shoes' as a model. Students write each 'a pair of ___' phrase by identifying the object in each picture. All seven answers are checked aloud together.

periods.teacher_notes: Task A requires students to think about real-world size and weight, not alphabetical order — if students alphabetise, redirect them gently by asking 'Which would weigh more in your hand?' For Task B, the word 'pair' connects directly back to the poem's 'only pair' of spectacles; drawing that link helps students remember the vocabulary in context.

periods.activity_title: Word Work — Spelling Check and Preposition Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p.5): identify and encircle the correctly spelt word from three options.
Let us Learn D (p.6): fill in prepositions in a short story using a word bank.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'watter / water / weter' on the board and asks which looks right and why. Students discuss the strategy of looking for familiar letter patterns rather than guessing.

Let us Learn C — students work through all ten spelling sets individually, encircling the correct word. Teacher circulates. Answers are reviewed aloud: teacher reads all three options, students call out the correct one, and the class examines why the other two are wrong.

Let us Learn D — teacher reads the short story on p.6 aloud once with blanks left silent. Students then read the word bank (around, after, before, in, above, on, among) and predict the preposition for each blank, writing answers in their notebooks.

Whole-class check of the preposition story: teacher reads each sentence, a student supplies the preposition and the class confirms. Teacher clarifies any confusion between 'above' and 'on', or 'before' and 'after', using spatial gestures.

periods.teacher_notes: Task C works best when students read each misspelling aloud — hearing 'elefant' versus 'elephant' helps them trust their phonological sense. For Task D, students who struggle may try all the prepositions from the word bank in turn; encourage them to read the sentence with each option and decide which sounds natural. 'Among' and 'around' are the two most likely to be swapped.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn E (pp.6–7): complete the antonyms crossword puzzle using clue sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains how a crossword works — Across clues run left to right, Down clues run top to bottom. Students open pp.6–7 and teacher walks through the sample clue 'Not far, it's ___' as a class, eliciting the answer 'near'.

Let us Learn E — students work through all ten clues individually or with a desk partner. Teacher circulates, offering hints by reading the clue aloud expressively rather than giving the answer directly.
Whole-class reveal: teacher reads each clue aloud and students call out answers. Each answer is written on the board and confirmed against the crossword grid. Students who have errors correct them.

Consolidation: teacher points to five answers on the board and asks students to say the opposite of each one — reinforcing the idea that these are antonyms. Students practise saying each pair aloud together.

periods.teacher_notes: The crossword clues are structured as antonym prompts — 'Not hot' → 'cold' — so students are practising opposite-word knowledge through context rather than memorisation. The most common error is writing answers that do not fit the grid's letter count; encourage students to count squares before writing. Clue Down 6 ('Not hot, she likes ___ coffee') and Across 6 ('I want ___ clothes') share the square for the letter 'c' — draw attention to this intersection so students can self-check.

periods.activity_title: Writing — Turn the Poem into a Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.8): retell the poem as a short story; draft, share and revise in class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models orally how to retell the poem's events as a story: 'Today, my father is unhappy. He has lost his spectacles — his only pair.' She writes two sentences on the board, thinking aloud about changing 'He can't read' into 'He was unable to read the newspaper'. Students notice what changes between poem and prose.

Shared planning: teacher guides the class to map the poem's four stanzas onto four story moments — the loss, the things he cannot do, the search, the discovery. Students jot three or four key words per moment in their notebooks.

Let us Write — students draft their story independently in their notebooks using the starter 'Today, my father is unhappy…'. Teacher circulates, offering a prompt question ('What did he do next?') to students who are stuck.

Paired share: each student reads her draft story to a desk partner. The partner identifies one moment that is described clearly and one that could be clearer. Students make one revision on their draft.
Two or three students read their revised stories aloud to the class. Teacher praises specific choices — a vivid verb, an added detail — and the class applauds each reader.

periods.teacher_notes: The key challenge is shifting from verse to prose — students may simply copy the poem's lines rather than retell them. The modelled oral step at the start is essential for showing what transformation looks like. Encourage students to add one detail the poem only implies, such as where Papa was sitting when he lost the spectacles, which develops their creative voice without departing from the story.

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text — Puzzles, Optical Illusions and a Riddle

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do A (p.9): move three matchsticks to make three squares.
Let us Do B (p.9): optical illusion — focus on red star, shift gaze to candle.
Let us Do C (p.10): find the hidden 'd' in the grid of 'b' letters.
Just for Fun (p.10): listen to the riddle and solve it aloud.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do A — teacher describes the matchstick puzzle on p.9 (four squares, move three matchsticks to make three squares). Students draw the arrangement in their notebooks and experiment. After individual attempts, volunteers share solutions and the class verifies.

Let us Do B — teacher guides the optical illusion activity on p.9: students focus their nose tip on the red star, then shift their gaze to the candle drawing. Students share their observation aloud. Teacher introduces the idea of an optical illusion briefly and connects it to how the poem's ending surprises us in a similar way.

Let us Do C — students open p.10 and search the grid of 'b' letters for the hidden 'd'. The task is individual and timed as an unhurried visual challenge. Students who find it quickly keep quiet until all have had a turn, then confirm the location together.

Just for Fun — teacher reads the riddle on p.10 aloud expressively ('I go to the market…'). Students think quietly, then whisper a guess to a neighbour before anyone calls out. The class discusses the answer together and students are invited to share any riddles they know from home.

periods.teacher_notes: The three hands-on activities in this sitting engage different kinds of attention — spatial reasoning, visual perception, and lateral thinking — and connect thematically to the poem's comedy of overlooked details. The optical illusion on p.9 is best done in near-silence with students' noses actually touching the page; the effect is stronger when they commit to the action. The riddle session at the close works well as a relaxed open exchange, so do not rush students toward the answer.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a humorous narrative poem using the poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Poem about Papa frantically searching for spectacles found on his own head.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 1 beginning "He can't read the newspaper". Which of the following best explains why Papa cannot do any of these things?

options.label: A
options.text: Papa has lost his spectacles and cannot see clearly without them.

options.label: B
options.text: Papa is angry and refuses to do any work.

options.label: C
options.text: Papa is feeling very tired and wants to rest.

options.label: D
options.text: Papa is waiting for the child to help him with everything.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have associated unhappiness in the poem with tiredness rather than poor vision.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have confused Papa's frustration with deliberate refusal, missing the cause in the poem.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have focused on the child's role in the final stanza without reading the earlier stanzas carefully.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a humorous narrative poem using the poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Poem about Papa frantically searching for spectacles found on his own head.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the child solves the problem by going up close to Papa and looking carefully. In your own words, write two sentences explaining what the child noticed and how that moment is funny.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The child noticed that Papa's spectacles were sitting right on top of his own head all along. It is funny because Papa searched everywhere except the most obvious place — his own head.

items.source_lo: Student discusses, narrates and discriminates sounds using guided conversation and listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Oral discussion on household chores, gratitude; sound-pair discrimination of homophones.
items.item_stem:
Your teacher will say two words aloud. Listen carefully and decide: do the words sound the same or different? For each pair below, write S (same) or D (different).
1. sun — son
2. bed — bad
3. hair — hare
4. cold — could
5. deer — dear

options.text: deer — dear sound the same (they are homophones).
hair — hare sound the same (they are homophones).
sun — son sound the same (they are homophones).

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — same (sun/son are homophones); 2 — different (bed/bad differ in the vowel sound); 3 — same (hair/hare are homophones); 4 — different (cold/could differ in the final consonant cluster); 5 — same (deer/dear are homophones).

items.item_stem: Think about the poem and your own life. Name two things that someone at your home cannot easily do without their spectacles or another helpful object. Then tell the class how you would thank a family member who helps you find something you have lost.

expected_elements: Names two realistic daily activities affected.
Connects at least one activity to home or family life.
Expresses thanks clearly in a complete spoken sentence.

items.source_lo: Student transforms a poem into short prose narrative using modelled writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Retelling the poem's four stanzas as a short story, starting from a given opening line.
items.item_stem:
Read the sentence below and decide if it is a good opening line for a story based on the poem. Write T (true) or F (false) and give one reason for your answer.
"Today, my father is unhappy because he cannot find his only pair of spectacles."

options.text: This sentence is a good opening line because it tells us who the story is about and what the problem is.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: True — the sentence introduces the main character (father), states his feeling (unhappy), and names the central problem (missing spectacles), which are the elements a good story opening needs.

items.source_lo: Student transforms a poem into short prose narrative using modelled writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Retelling the poem's four stanzas as a short story, starting from a given opening line.
items.item_stem: Write a short story of four to six sentences based on the poem. Begin with: 'Today, my father is unhappy…' Make sure your story includes what Papa could not do, where he searched, and how the child helped him.

expected_elements: Story states at least one thing Papa could not do.
Story names at least one place where Papa searched.
Child's role in finding the spectacles is included.

items.item_stem:
The word 'pair' appears in the poem when the child says Papa has lost 'his only pair'. Choose the correct preposition to complete each sentence below. Write the answers in your notebook.
1. My father looked for his spectacles ________ the newspapers on the table. (among / above / before)
2. He searched all ________ the house before finally giving up. (around / after / in)
3. His spectacles were sitting ________ his head the whole time! (on / before / among)

items.item_stem: Listen to this riddle: 'I go to the market, I lovingly bring you home, I sit in front of you, and I cry, cry, cry. What am I?' Say your answer aloud and explain in one or two sentences why you think that answer is correct.
